topics.title: 5.1.1 Accounting for Member Storage
topics.summary: sizeof reports the size of an object representation in bytes, including any padding needed for its type. A class containing several members is not guaranteed to occupy exactly the sum of their sizes. Arrays also require each element to begin at a suitable alignment, so a type’s size supports the stride between array elements.

blocks.text: sizeof(T) reports the size of an object of type T in C++ bytes, including storage needed to satisfy layout and array-stride requirements. It is not necessarily the total memory retained by everything the object owns. A std::string object can own a separate character allocation; a vector object can own a separate element buffer. Summing sizeof over top-level owners can therefore substantially undercount a live object graph.

blocks.text: Arrays explain why trailing padding can matter. Every element must begin at a suitable alignment for its type. The complete-object size determines the stride between adjacent elements, so it must support valid placement of each element. A layout with a member near the end may therefore include trailing padding even when no following member needs it inside the same object. The next array element is the relevant neighbor.

topics.title: 5.1.2 Recognizing Compiler-Inserted Padding
topics.summary: Padding can appear between members or at the end of a class to satisfy alignment and layout requirements. Reordering members can change padding on a particular implementation, but it may also affect readability, ABI compatibility, or cache behavior. A smaller sizeof is not automatically a better public layout if compatibility or access patterns matter more.

blocks.text: Padding bytes do not represent meaningful application fields and should not be used for logical equality. Comparing entire object representations with memcmp can report differences between logically equal values because padding need not have a stable value. It can also mishandle types with multiple representations for equivalent values. Compare fields or use a defined value comparison.

blocks.text: Padding is storage that supports representation and alignment but does not necessarily carry a member’s logical value. A compiler can insert it between members or at the end of the object. Two records with equal member values can have different padding bytes, so a raw byte comparison is not generally an appropriate implementation of value equality.

blocks.text: Consider two independently constructed records with the same tag, count, and value. A member-wise comparison asks the domain question: do the fields represent equal values? memcmp asks whether every compared representation byte is equal. Those questions can differ because of padding and because some types have multiple representations with related value semantics. Floating-point positive and negative zero illustrate why even an apparently meaningful bit difference need not match the intended equality contract.

blocks.text: Padding also matters when exporting memory. A raw structure dump can include bytes that the application never intended to serialize. Even when the dump appears stable in a local test, it couples the format to compiler layout and risks disclosing incidental representation data. An explicit encoder writes only named fields in a specified order and width. That is both a compatibility improvement and a clearer information boundary.

blocks.text: Field reordering can reduce gaps on one ABI, but it is not free when layout is part of an interface. A structure shared with another library, mapped file, or binary protocol may have an established contract. Changing order to save a few bytes can break that contract. Prefer keeping external formats independent of private in-memory layout so internal optimization does not require a coordinated wire-format change.

blocks.text: Avoid applying packing pragmas as a universal repair. A packed layout can introduce unaligned fields and platform-specific access costs or restrictions. Even when the compiler supports packed accesses, taking a pointer to a packed member and using it as an ordinarily aligned typed pointer can create additional hazards. The safer beginner’s approach is to decode external bytes into a normal domain object, then perform computation through that object’s valid typed interface.

topics.title: 5.2.1 Understanding Standard-Layout Types
topics.summary: Standard-layout is a language category with restrictions intended to support predictable structural relationships and interoperability uses. It is not a promise that every compiler gives the type the same offsets, size, or ABI. Facilities such as offsetof have defined applicability tied to layout rules; use them on appropriate types rather than arbitrary polymorphic classes.

topics.title: 5.2.2 Understanding Trivially Copyable Types
topics.summary: Trivially copyable types support certain representation-copy operations specified by the language. Copying their bytes into another existing object of the same type through memcpy can preserve the value under the applicable rules. This differs from copying the bytes of std::string or unique_ptr, whose invariants and ownership cannot be duplicated by raw memory copying.

topics.title: Failure clinic — The structure changed but the file format did not
topics.summary: A developer adds a field to an internal record and rebuilds the writer. Old readers still consume the same number of bytes and interpret them with the previous layout. The defect is not necessarily in the new field’s value; it is the absence of an explicit versioned encoding contract. Repair the serialization boundary rather than asking every reader to guess which native layout produced a file.
